title: How a care agent knows when to ask a human
subtitle: A LangGraph workflow texts patients through a home treatment; a judge agent sends tricky turns to human reviewers.
hook: The judge docks confidence for complexity, not just doubt, so any turn under 75% waits for a human.

sources.title: Case Study + Deep Dive: Telemedicine Support Agents with LangGraph/MCP
sources.speaker: Dan Mason

nodes.label: Patient
nodes.detail: A patient taking a home medication regimen texts updates and questions in their own words. The agent only runs when the patient sends a message; reminders scheduled earlier cover the silences.
nodes.tradeoff: Reminders stop after one or two nudges and nothing polls the patient, so the system stays low touch.

nodes.label: Text gateway
nodes.detail: A Node service on AWS takes texts in through Twilio, hands the patient's state to the agent graph, and sends approved replies, including MMS images with dates stamped on.
nodes.tradeoff: The LLM side only ever sees a first name; phone numbers and other identifiers stay in this box.

nodes.label: Schedule document
nodes.detail: A versioned per-patient snapshot: messages so far, unsent scheduled messages, anchors (events that did or will happen) and time zone. It is loaded at the start of a turn and saved back at the end.
nodes.tradeoff: Each turn restarts from this compressed state; long-running threads led to forgotten tool calls and JSON errors.

nodes.label: Virtual ops associate
nodes.detail: One Claude agent in a LangGraph container reads the state and the blueprint, then proposes the next texts, anchor changes and scheduled reminders, each with a written rationale.
nodes.tradeoff: It stays one agent instead of several smaller ones, because switching system prompts breaks Claude's prompt cache.

nodes.label: Treatment blueprints
nodes.detail: Each treatment is a set of cross-linked markdown files, edited in Google Docs with a physician assistant: an overview, one file per phase, a triage guide and a Q&A list, read through an MCP file server.
nodes.tradeoff: No RAG: the agent reads whole documents, because retrieved snippets could not capture the shape of a treatment.

nodes.label: Evaluator agent
nodes.detail: A second agent with its own prompt checks the proposal against the guidelines, then scores it. It deducts for complexity: new anchors, edited patient data, several or duplicate messages.
nodes.tradeoff: LLMs are hard to convince they are wrong, so judging complexity is the easier, more reliable signal.

nodes.label: Human reviewer
nodes.detail: Below the 75% threshold, an operations associate sees the proposal and rationale in a dashboard, then approves it or types feedback in plain English, which resumes the same graph thread.
nodes.tradeoff: They see roughly one in ten exchanges, and an approval takes about as long as the old button press.

nodes.label: LangSmith traces
nodes.detail: The full back-and-forth between the two agents, with every tool call, is kept in LangSmith as a debugging record. Only each turn's input and output go back to the main system.
nodes.tradeoff: Its cost view ignores prompt caching, so it overstates spend; caching brings a message to about 15 to 20 cents.

nodes.label: Offline evals
nodes.detail: A custom harness pulls datasets from LangSmith, rewrites old timestamps, replays them through the graph, and has a GPT-4o rubric judge whether the output state matches.
nodes.tradeoff: The rubric is deliberately fuzzy: it flags anything completely broken and ignores harmless wording changes.

flow.text: Says the medicine arrived and gives their local time.
Loads the patient's schedule document and starts a graph run.
Reads the blueprint, sets the time zone, schedules the next messages.
Docks points for many changes at once; confidence lands at 70%.
Below 75%, an associate asks it to use the patient's name.
Resumes the same thread and rewrites only that message.
After approval, sends the texts and saves the new state.

takeaways.text: Treatments live in documents, not code, so a new regimen ships without new software.
A judge with its own prompt is a second bite at the apple, mostly by spotting complexity.
Skip RAG when the model must grasp a whole process; give it the complete documents.
